claim: Type I and type III interferon (IFN) are virus-induced cytokines that potently restrict viral replication during the first days of infection before activation of the adaptive immune system occurs.
source: Type I and type III interferon (IFN) are virus-induced cytokines that potently restrict viral replication during the first days of infection before activation of the adaptive immune system occurs (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015).

claim: The type I IFN family consists of several IFN-α subtypes, a single IFN-β and several minor family members that all bind to and act via the IFN-α/β receptor complex (IFNAR).
source: The type I IFN family consists of several IFN-α subtypes, a single IFN-β and several minor family members that all bind to and act via the IFN-α/β receptor complex (IFNAR), which is expressed on most nucleated cells (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015) with the possible exception of intestinal epithelial cells (Lin et al., 2016; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015).

claim: The IFN-α/β receptor complex (IFNAR) is expressed on most nucleated cells with the possible exception of intestinal epithelial cells.
source: The type I IFN family consists of several IFN-α subtypes, a single IFN-β and several minor family members that all bind to and act via the IFN-α/β receptor complex (IFNAR), which is expressed on most nucleated cells (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015) with the possible exception of intestinal epithelial cells (Lin et al., 2016; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2016; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015).

claim: The members of the type III IFN family (IFN-λ) bind to a different receptor complex (IFN-λ receptor; IFNLR).
source: The members of the type III IFN family (IFN-λ) bind to a different receptor complex (IFN-λ receptor; IFNLR), which is highly expressed on epithelial cells (Kotenko et al., 2003; Lazear et al., 2015; Sheppard et al., 2003; Sommereyns et al., 2008; Wack et al., 2015) and neutrophils (Blazek et al., 2015; Broggi et al., 2017; Espinosa et al., 2017; Galani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kotenko et al., 2003; Lazear et al., 2015; Sheppard et al., 2003; Sommereyns et al., 2008; Wack et al., 2015).

claim: The IFN-λ receptor complex is highly expressed on epithelial cells.
source: The members of the type III IFN family (IFN-λ) bind to a different receptor complex (IFN-λ receptor; IFNLR), which is highly expressed on epithelial cells (Kotenko et al., 2003; Lazear et al., 2015; Sheppard et al., 2003; Sommereyns et al., 2008; Wack et al., 2015) and neutrophils (Blazek et al., 2015; Broggi et al., 2017; Espinosa et al., 2017; Galani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kotenko et al., 2003; Lazear et al., 2015; Sheppard et al., 2003; Sommereyns et al., 2008; Wack et al., 2015).

claim: The IFN-λ receptor complex is highly expressed on neutrophils.
source: The members of the type III IFN family (IFN-λ) bind to a different receptor complex (IFN-λ receptor; IFNLR), which is highly expressed on epithelial cells (Kotenko et al., 2003; Lazear et al., 2015; Sheppard et al., 2003; Sommereyns et al., 2008; Wack et al., 2015) and neutrophils (Blazek et al., 2015; Broggi et al., 2017; Espinosa et al., 2017; Galani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Blazek et al., 2015; Broggi et al., 2017; Espinosa et al., 2017; Galani et al., 2017).

claim: Influenza virus replication is strongly restricted by IFN-regulated Mx genes.
source: Influenza virus replication is strongly restricted by IFN-regulated Mx genes (Haller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Haller et al., 2015).

claim: Most standard inbred mouse strains carry defective Mx alleles.
source: Since most standard inbred mouse strains carry defective Mx alleles (Haller et al., 2015), the full magnitude of influenza virus restriction by the IFN system only becomes apparent when mouse strains carrying functional Mx1 alleles derived from wild mice are employed (Haller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Haller et al., 2015).

claim: Type I IFN plays a prominent role in the defense against respiratory viruses, including influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus or human metapneumovirus.
source: Using these knockout mouse strains we demonstrated that type I IFN plays a prominent role in the defense against respiratory viruses, including influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus or human metapneumovirus, whereas protection mediated by IFN-λ was surprisingly small (Mordstein et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Mordstein et al., 2010b).

claim: Protection mediated by IFN-λ against respiratory viruses was surprisingly small in previous studies.
source: Using these knockout mouse strains we demonstrated that type I IFN plays a prominent role in the defense against respiratory viruses, including influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus or human metapneumovirus, whereas protection mediated by IFN-λ was surprisingly small (Mordstein et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Mordstein et al., 2010b).

claim: The protective role of IFN-λ during viral infections of the small intestine was found to be far more pronounced than that of type I IFN.
source: In contrast, the protective role of IFN-λ during viral infections of the small intestine was found to be far more pronounced than that of type I IFN (Baldridge et al., 2017; Baldridge et al., 2015; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015; Nice et al., 2015; Pott et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Baldridge et al., 2017; Baldridge et al., 2015; Mahlakõiv et al., 2015; Nice et al., 2015; Pott et al., 2011).

claim: IFN-λ is produced more quickly than type I IFN in influenza virus-infected mice.
source: Recent work with influenza virus-infected mice (Galani et al., 2017) indicated that IFN-λ is produced more quickly than type I IFN, suggesting that IFN-λ plays a non-redundant role in suppressing early virus growth in the respiratory tract.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Galani et al., 2017).

claim: Protective effects of IFN-λ were observed only if very low infection doses were used in previous studies.
source: Nevertheless, protective effects of IFN-λ were observed only if very low infection doses were used, presumably because mice with defective Mx1 alleles were employed for these studies.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from previous studies and the authors' knowledge of experimental conditions.

claim: According to standard protocols for experimental influenza virus infections, the virus is delivered intranasally to anesthetized mice in a 40–50 µl volume, allowing immediate infection of the entire respiratory tract.
source: According to standard protocols for experimental influenza virus infections, the virus is delivered intranasally to anesthetized mice in a 40–50 µl volume, allowing immediate infection of the entire respiratory tract.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of standard experimental protocols.

claim: Standard experimental setup might override the natural barrier function of the nasal mucosa by allowing the infection to artificially initiate in the lower respiratory tract.
source: This experimental setup might override the natural barrier function of the nasal mucosa by allowing the infection to artificially initiate in the lower respiratory tract (Ivinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ivinson et al., 2017).

claim: When 104 PFU of the H7N7 influenza A virus strain SC35M was applied intranasally in a standard 40 µl volume, Ifnlr1−/− mice supported similar virus replication in the lungs on day three post infection compared with wild-type animals.
source: Similarly, when we applied 104 PFU of the H7N7 influenza A virus strain SC35M intranasally in a standard 40 µl volume, we noted that Mx1-competent animals carrying a defective IFN-λ receptor (Ifnlr1−/−) supported similar virus replication in the lungs on day three post infection, compared with Mx1-competent wild-type (WT) animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ifnar1−/− mice showed significantly elevated viral titers in the lungs compared to wild-type mice when infected with SC35M in a 40 µl volume.
source: In contrast, Mx1-competent mice lacking functional type I IFN receptors (Ifnar1−/−) showed significantly elevated viral titers under such experimental conditions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Virus delivery can be targeted specifically to the upper respiratory tract of mice if the inoculum is applied in a volume of 10 µl.
source: Using poliovirus that is unable to infect mouse cells as an indicator we found that virus delivery can be targeted specifically to the upper respiratory tract of mice if the inoculum is applied in a volume of 10 µl (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A large proportion of the inoculum reached the lungs if the inoculum was applied in a volume of 40 µl.
source: In contrast, a large proportion of the inoculum reached the lungs if the inoculum was applied in a volume of 40 µl.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a 10 µl volume was used to deliver influenza virus strain SC35M specifically to the upper respiratory tract of WT mice, the virus grew well in the upper airways, but was absent or present at only very low titers in the tracheae (3 of 22 animals) and the lungs (1 of 22 animals) on day five post-infection.
source: When a 10 µl volume was used to deliver influenza virus strain SC35M specifically to the upper respiratory tract of WT mice, the virus grew well in the upper airways, but was absent or present at only very low titers in the tracheae (3 of 22 animals) and the lungs (1 of 22 animals) on day five post-infection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Ifnlr1−/− mice infected with SC35M via 10 µl delivery, viral titers in the upper airways were significantly higher than in WT mice and many infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contained high virus levels in the tracheae (11/23) and lungs (13/23).
source: In Ifnlr1−/− mice, viral titers in the upper airways were significantly higher than in WT mice and, most interestingly, many infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contained high virus levels in the tracheae (11/23) and lungs (13/23) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ifnar1−/− mice had significantly higher virus titers in the upper airways than WT mice when infected with SC35M via 10 µl delivery, and more animals contained virus in the tracheae (5/23) and lungs (9/23).
source: As expected, Ifnar1−/− mice also had significantly higher virus titers in the upper airways than WT mice, and more animals contained virus in the tracheae (5/23) and lungs (9/23) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ifnar1−/− mice seemed to control the virus spread from the upper airways to the lungs slightly better than Ifnlr1−/− mice.
source: In comparison, Ifnar1−/− mice seemed to control the virus spread from the upper airways to the lungs slightly better than Ifnlr1−/− mice (Figure 1B), indicating that IFN-λ is more potent in containing viral infections within the upper respiratory tract than type I IFN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IFN-λ is more potent in containing viral infections within the upper respiratory tract than type I IFN.
source: In comparison, Ifnar1−/− mice seemed to control the virus spread from the upper airways to the lungs slightly better than Ifnlr1−/− mice (Figure 1B), indicating that IFN-λ is more potent in containing viral infections within the upper respiratory tract than type I IFN.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After selective delivery of Udorn virus to the upper respiratory tract, Udorn virus was rarely found in the tracheae (1/16) or lungs (0/16) of WT mice.
source: After selective delivery to the upper respiratory tract, Udorn virus was rarely found in the tracheae (1/16) or lungs (0/16) of WT mice, but was frequently present in the tracheae (15/16) and lungs (14/16) of Ifnlr1−/− mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After selective delivery of Udorn virus to the upper respiratory tract, Udorn virus was frequently present in the tracheae (15/16) and lungs (14/16) of Ifnlr1−/− mice.
source: After selective delivery to the upper respiratory tract, Udorn virus was rarely found in the tracheae (1/16) or lungs (0/16) of WT mice, but was frequently present in the tracheae (15/16) and lungs (14/16) of Ifnlr1−/− mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ifnar1−/− mice showed an intermediate phenotype for Udorn virus spread, with infectious virus found at lower frequency in the tracheae (8/15) and lungs (9/15) compared with Ifnlr1−/− mice.
source: Ifnar1−/− mice showed an intermediate phenotype under these experimental conditions, and infectious virus was found at lower frequency in the tracheae (8/15) and lungs (9/15) of Ifnar1−/− mice compared with Ifnlr1−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SeV reached the lungs of all (15/15) Ifnlr1−/− mice when selectively applied to the upper respiratory tract.
source: A similar picture emerged when a murine respiratory virus (Sendai virus; SeV) was employed in infection experiments. SeV reached the lungs of all (15/15) Ifnlr1−/− mice when selectively applied to the upper respiratory tract (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SeV reached the lungs of WT mice at significantly reduced frequency (6/15) compared to Ifnlr1−/− mice when selectively applied to the upper respiratory tract.
source: In contrast, SeV reached the lungs of WT mice at significantly reduced frequency (6/15) under these experimental conditions, and virus titers at day five post-infection in the lungs of WT mice were generally lower compared with Ifnlr1−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Virus titers at day five post-infection in the lungs of WT mice were generally lower compared with Ifnlr1−/− mice for SeV infection.
source: In contrast, SeV reached the lungs of WT mice at significantly reduced frequency (6/15) under these experimental conditions, and virus titers at day five post-infection in the lungs of WT mice were generally lower compared with Ifnlr1−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IFN-λ is an indispensable antiviral cytokine that restricts respiratory viral infections to the upper airways and limits virus spread to the lungs.
source: Taken together, these data clearly indicated that IFN-λ is an indispensable antiviral cytokine that restricts respiratory viral infections to the upper airways and limits virus spread to the lungs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figures 1B, 1C, and 1D.

claim: Expression of the IFN-λ2 and IFN-λ3 genes was significantly reduced in snout tissue of Ifnar1−/− mice compared with WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice.
source: Expression of the IFN-λ2 and IFN-λ3 genes was significantly reduced in snout tissue of Ifnar1−/− mice compared with WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice, whereas baseline expression of IFN-α and IFN-β genes was comparable (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Baseline expression of IFN-α and IFN-β genes was comparable across WT, Ifnar1−/−, and Ifnlr1−/− mice.
source: Expression of the IFN-λ2 and IFN-λ3 genes was significantly reduced in snout tissue of Ifnar1−/− mice compared with WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice, whereas baseline expression of IFN-α and IFN-β genes was comparable (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Baseline expression of the Mx1 gene was lower in snout tissue of Ifnar1−/− mice than in WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice.
source: Consequently, baseline expression of the Mx1 gene was also lower in snout tissue of Ifnar1−/− mice than in WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon infection with Udorn virus, expression of the IFN-λ genes in Ifnar1−/− mice returned to comparable levels of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice within two days.
source: Upon infection with Udorn virus, expression of the IFN-λ genes in Ifnar1−/− mice returned to comparable levels of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice within two days (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of the IFN-λ genes in snout homogenates of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice was only slightly induced after virus infection.
source: Interestingly, expression of the IFN-λ genes in snout homogenates of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice was only slightly induced after virus infection, whereas expression of the IFN-β gene was induced about tenfold in all mouse strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of the IFN-β gene was induced about tenfold in all mouse strains after Udorn virus infection.
source: Interestingly, expression of the IFN-λ genes in snout homogenates of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice was only slightly induced after virus infection, whereas expression of the IFN-β gene was induced about tenfold in all mouse strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Functional type I IFN signaling is needed for proper baseline expression of the IFN-λ genes, which contributes to early virus defense in the upper airways.
source: These data indicate that functional type I IFN signaling is needed for proper baseline expression of the IFN-λ genes, which contributes to early virus defense in the upper airways.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: When the infection was initiated by applying the inoculum selectively to the upper airways, none of the influenza viruses used in this study caused morbidity or mortality, although virus titers in lungs of Ifnlr1−/− mice reached levels above 106 PFU in some animals on day five post-infection.
source: When the infection was initiated by applying the inoculum selectively to the upper airways, none of the influenza viruses used in this study caused morbidity or mortality, although virus titers in lungs of Ifnlr1−/− mice reached levels above 106 PFU in some animals on day five post-infection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Upper airway infections with influenza viruses are usually benign in mice presumably because saliva components delay the spread of influenza viruses to the lungs.
source: These observations are in good agreement with recent work indicating that upper airway infections with influenza viruses are usually benign in mice presumably because saliva components delay the spread of influenza viruses to the lungs (Ivinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ivinson et al., 2017).

claim: Delayed virus arrival in the lungs may permit timely adaptive immune responses to eliminate the virus before it causes irreversible tissue damage.
source: Delayed virus arrival in the lungs may permit timely adaptive immune responses to eliminate the virus before it causes irreversible tissue damage.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism underlying the benign nature of upper airway infections.

claim: The upper airway infection model is not suitable for studying influenza virus-induced pathology in mice.
source: We concluded from these observations that the upper airway infection model is not suitable for studying influenza virus-induced pathology in mice, but it allows addressing the question which factors might control virus growth at the entry site.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The upper airway infection model allows addressing the question which factors might control virus growth at the entry site.
source: We concluded from these observations that the upper airway infection model is not suitable for studying influenza virus-induced pathology in mice, but it allows addressing the question which factors might control virus growth at the entry site.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Ifnlr1−/− mice shed significantly more infectious Udorn virus than WT or Ifnar1−/− mice.
source: This analysis revealed that Ifnlr1−/− mice shed significantly more infectious virus than WT or Ifnar1−/− mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Already at 12 hr post infection, Ifnlr1−/− mice secreted remarkable amounts of infectious Udorn virus.
source: Already at 12 hr post infection, Ifnlr1−/− mice secreted remarkable amounts of infectious virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Virus shedding of Udorn was only transient and peaked between 24 and 36 hr post infection.
source: Interestingly, virus shedding was only transient and peaked between 24 and 36 hr post infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At least 10-fold more infectious SeV was found in mucosal secretions of Ifnlr1−/− mice compared with WT controls between days 2 and 4 post infection.
source: When the nostrils of SeV-infected mice were swabbed (Figure 3B), we found at least 10-fold more infectious SeV in mucosal secretions of Ifnlr1−/− mice compared with WT controls between days 2 and 4 post infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Levels of infectious SeV in mucosal secretions of Ifnar1−/− mice were only slightly increased compared with WT mice.
source: Levels of infectious SeV in mucosal secretions of Ifnar1−/− mice were only slightly increased compared with WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ifnar1−/− mice shed significantly less SeV than Ifnlr1−/− mice at all time points between days 2 and 4 post infection.
source: Importantly, Ifnar1−/− mice shed significantly less virus than Ifnlr1−/− mice at all time points between days 2 and 4 post infection (Figure 3B), indicating that IFN-λ is the dominant limiting factor for virus shedding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IFN-λ is the dominant limiting factor for virus shedding.
source: Importantly, Ifnar1−/− mice shed significantly less virus than Ifnlr1−/− mice at all time points between days 2 and 4 post infection (Figure 3B), indicating that IFN-λ is the dominant limiting factor for virus shedding.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 79% of the sentinels that were in contact with Udorn-infected Ifnlr1−/− mice became infected.
source: Under such experimental conditions, 79% of the sentinels that were in contact with infected Ifnlr1−/− mice became infected (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Transmission of Udorn to sentinel mice was observed much less frequently (17% and 42%, respectively) when infected WT or Ifnar1−/− mice were employed as virus spreaders.
source: As expected from the virus excretion data (Figure 3A), transmission of Udorn to sentinel mice was observed much less frequently (17% and 42%, respectively) when infected WT or Ifnar1−/− mice were employed as virus spreaders (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 10 of 11 (91%) sentinels in contact with HK68-infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus.
source: Under these experimental conditions, 10 of 11 (91%) sentinels in contact with infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus, whereas only 27% of the sentinels cohoused either with infected WT or Ifnar1−/− mice became infected (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only 27% of the sentinels cohoused either with HK68-infected WT or Ifnar1−/− mice became infected.
source: Under these experimental conditions, 10 of 11 (91%) sentinels in contact with infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus, whereas only 27% of the sentinels cohoused either with infected WT or Ifnar1−/− mice became infected (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All sentinels co-housed with SeV-infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus.
source: All sentinels co-housed with SeV-infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus, whereas only 38% of the sentinels cohoused with WT mice and 75% of the sentinels cohoused with Ifnar1−/− became infected with SeV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Only 38% of the sentinels cohoused with SeV-infected WT mice became infected with SeV.
source: All sentinels co-housed with SeV-infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus, whereas only 38% of the sentinels cohoused with WT mice and 75% of the sentinels cohoused with Ifnar1−/− became infected with SeV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 75% of the sentinels cohoused with SeV-infected Ifnar1−/− mice became infected with SeV.
source: All sentinels co-housed with SeV-infected Ifnlr1−/− mice contracted the virus, whereas only 38% of the sentinels cohoused with WT mice and 75% of the sentinels cohoused with Ifnar1−/− became infected with SeV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IFN-λ effectively limits the spread of respiratory viruses in a contact transmission setting.
source: Together, these data show that IFN-λ effectively limits the spread of respiratory viruses in a contact transmission setting.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, and 4C.

claim: Endogenous IFN-λ confers better protection against influenza virus infection compared with type I IFN if very low viral doses are used.
source: A recent study in mice suggests that endogenous IFN-λ confers better protection against influenza virus infection compared with type I IFN if very low viral doses are used (Galani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Galani et al., 2017).

claim: When the challenge dose of Udorn was reduced to 100 PFU per animal, the differences in the upper airways of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice became more obvious.
source: Indeed, when the challenge dose of Udorn was reduced to 100 PFU per animal, the differences in the upper airways of WT and Ifnlr1−/− mice became more obvious (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Replication of Udorn in the upper airways was not increased in Ifnar1−/− animals when compared with WT mice at low infection doses.
source: In agreement with the virus excretion data (Figure 3), which had indicated a minor role for type I IFN in this process, replication of Udorn in the upper airways was not increased in Ifnar1−/− animals when compared with WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), supporting the view that IFN-λ plays a more prominent role in antiviral protection of the upper respiratory tract than type I IFN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFN-λ plays a more prominent role in antiviral protection of the upper respiratory tract than type I IFN.
source: In agreement with the virus excretion data (Figure 3), which had indicated a minor role for type I IFN in this process, replication of Udorn in the upper airways was not increased in Ifnar1−/− animals when compared with WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), supporting the view that IFN-λ plays a more prominent role in antiviral protection of the upper respiratory tract than type I IFN.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hybrid IFN-αB/D and mouse IFN-λ2 can induce the IFN-responsive genes Isg15, Stat1 and Mx1 to similar levels if used at identical concentrations in differentiated primary mouse airway epithelial cell cultures.
source: Pilot experiments with differentiated primary mouse airway epithelial cell cultures, known to express functional receptors for both type I and type III IFN (Crotta et al., 2013), demonstrated that hybrid IFN-αB/D and mouse IFN-λ2 can induce the IFN-responsive genes Isg15, Stat1 and Mx1 to similar levels if used at identical concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: IFN-λ pretreatment potently inhibited Udorn virus replication in the upper airways, whereas IFN-α pretreatment had no such effect.
source: IFN-λ pretreatment potently inhibited virus replication in the upper airways, whereas IFN-α pretreatment had no such effect (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The differences between IFN-α and IFN-λ in inhibiting Udorn virus replication were far less pronounced in the lungs than in the upper airways.
source: Of note, the differences between IFN-α and IFN-λ were far less pronounced in the lungs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Viral titers in the upper airway of IFN-λ-treated mice were on average about 5-fold lower than in mock- or IFN-α-treated mice on day six post infection with SeV.
source: On day six post infection with SeV, viral titers in the upper airway of IFN-λ-treated mice were on average about 5-fold lower than in mock- or IFN-α-treated mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only 33% (3/9) of the IFN-λ-treated mice transmitted SeV to sentinel animals.
source: Only 33% (3/9) of the IFN-λ-treated mice transmitted SeV to sentinel animals, whereas 67% (6/9) of the IFN-α-treated mice infected the sentinels upon co-housing (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 67% (6/9) of the IFN-α-treated mice transmitted SeV to sentinel animals upon co-housing.
source: Only 33% (3/9) of the IFN-λ-treated mice transmitted SeV to sentinel animals, whereas 67% (6/9) of the IFN-α-treated mice infected the sentinels upon co-housing (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mock-treated WT mice transmitted SeV at a frequency of 88% (7/8).
source: Mock-treated WT mice transmitted SeV at a frequency of 88% (7/8) under the same conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IFN-λ is able to inhibit virus replication in the upper respiratory tract to a much greater extent than IFN-α.
source: Taken together, these experiments demonstrated that IFN-λ is able to inhibit virus replication in the upper respiratory tract to a much greater extent than IFN-α.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 5A, 5B, and 5C.

claim: Only IFN-λ strongly decreased the rate of successful virus transmission to cage mates.
source: Furthermore, only IFN-λ strongly decreased the rate of successful virus transmission to cage mates.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IFN-λ applied subcutaneously provided strong and long-lasting protection against SeV in the upper airways and lungs of mice.
source: IFN-λ applied subcutaneously provided strong and long-lasting protection against SeV in the upper airways and lungs of mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IFN-α-treated animals sacrificed on either day 4 or six post infection had similar levels of SeV in nasal swabs and upper airways as mock-treated mice.
source: In contrast, IFN-α-treated animals sacrificed on either day 4 or six post infection had similar levels of SeV in nasal swabs and upper airways as mock-treated mice, but the IFN-α-treated animals contained reduced viral titers in the lungs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IFN-α-treated animals contained reduced viral titers in the lungs at days 4 and 6 post SeV infection.
source: In contrast, IFN-α-treated animals sacrificed on either day 4 or six post infection had similar levels of SeV in nasal swabs and upper airways as mock-treated mice, but the IFN-α-treated animals contained reduced viral titers in the lungs (Figure 6A).
